a: his days were many
p: The Hebrew says David "had come into the days," an idiom for old age.
b: The Hebrew says that David was old and "had come into the days" (ba' bayyamim), the same phrase used of Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 18:11; 24:1) and of Joshua (Joshua 13:1). David was about seventy (2 Samuel 5:4). Since Kings joins straight on to 2 Samuel, the Greek and Latin Bibles call this book 3 Kingdoms or 3 Kings; the story of David's court that began in 2 Samuel 9–20 reaches its end here.
orig: בָּא בַּיָּמִים (ba' bayyamim), "come into the days"

a: his servants
p: The Hebrew eved means anyone under a master: a slave, a court official, or a polite "I" before a king.
b: Eved covers a wide range. Shimei's runaway "slaves" (2:39) are property. The king's "servants" here are his courtiers and officials. And when Nathan says "me, your servant" (1:26), it is the polite way to say "I" to a king; Bathsheba uses the feminine word, amah, "your servant" (1:13, 1:17). This translation says "servant" or "slave" by context. Kings also calls David "my servant" in God's mouth (11:13), a title of honor, as with Moses (8:53).

a: She will attend the king and look after him
p: The rare word sokhenet means someone who looks after things: a nurse, an attendant, or a steward.
b: The word sokhenet is the feminine of soken, the title of Shebna, the palace steward, in Isaiah 22:15. So Abishag may be more than a bed-warmer: an attendant with real standing at court. That would help explain why Adonijah later wants her (2:17) and why Solomon hears the request as a claim to the throne (2:22). Josephus says the king's doctors gave this advice (Antiquities 7.343). Warming the old with a young body was also a medical practice known in the ancient world.

a: Abishag the Shunammite
p: Shunem was a village in the valley of Jezreel, later home of the woman who helped Elisha.
b: Shunem lay on the slope of the Hill of Moreh above the valley of Jezreel, in the territory of Issachar (Joshua 19:18). The Philistines camped there before Saul's last battle (1 Samuel 28:4), and Elisha stayed there with a rich woman whose son he raised (2 Kings 4:8–37). Some scholars have linked the "Shulammite" of Song of Songs 6:13 with Abishag the Shunammite, since the Song is tied to Solomon; the link is possible but unproven.
r: Joshua 19:18; 1 Samuel 28:4; 2 Kings 4:8; Song of Songs 6:13

a: the king did not sleep with her
t: A test of the king's strength?
p: The narrator notes that David did not have sex with Abishag. Many readers think this shows he could no longer rule.
b: The Hebrew says the king "did not know her," the usual idiom for sex (Genesis 4:1). The remark has two jobs. It makes plain that Abishag was not David's wife or concubine, which matters when Adonijah asks for her (2:17). And many scholars, such as John Gray and Mordechai Cogan, read it as a sign that the king's strength, on which the land's well-being was thought to depend, was gone: the next verse begins at once with Adonijah's bid. Others think the narrator only means to show David's age and loneliness. Jewish tradition (Bavli Sanhedrin 22a) imagines Abishag asking David to marry her and David refusing because he already had the full number of wives allowed a king.

a: He got himself a chariot and horsemen, and fifty men ran in front of him
p: Adonijah copies his older brother Absalom, who began his revolt with a chariot and fifty runners.
b: The words echo 2 Samuel 15:1: "Absalom acquired a chariot and horses for himself, and fifty men who ran in front of him" (2 Samuel 15:1). The reader knows how that story ended. Runners before a chariot were a public show of royal rank, as Samuel had warned (1 Samuel 8:11). Adonijah was David's fourth son (2 Samuel 3:4); with Amnon, Absalom and probably Chileab gone, he was the oldest living son, and he expected the throne (2:15).

a: His father had never in his life corrected him
p: The narrator blames David's failure to discipline his sons, as with Amnon and Absalom.
b: The verb atsav means to hurt or grieve; David never "pained" Adonijah by asking him to account for himself. The same weakness shows when David is angry at Amnon but will not "bring pain" to him (2 Samuel 13:21), and when he lets Absalom come home without justice (2 Samuel 14:33). Readers since the rabbis have drawn the lesson of Proverbs 13:24. Others notice that the narrator also says Adonijah was handsome and next in line after Absalom: like Saul and Absalom, a fine-looking man who was not chosen (1 Samuel 9:2; 2 Samuel 14:25).

a: He made his plans with Joab son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar the priest
p: Adonijah's side is David's old guard from Hebron; Solomon's side is made up of men who rose in Jerusalem.
b: Joab had led David's army since Hebron, and Abiathar had been David's priest since he fled Saul (1 Samuel 22:20–23). Both were Judahites of long standing. On the other side, Zadok first appears in Samuel after the capture of Jerusalem (2 Samuel 8:17, where the site's Plain, following the Hebrew, names "Ahimelech son of Abiathar" beside him); Chronicles places a young warrior named Zadok with David at Hebron (1 Chronicles 12:28), Benaiah commanded the foreign bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18), and Nathan was the court prophet. Many historians, such as Tomoo Ishida, see a struggle between the old Hebron circle and a newer Jerusalem circle. The narrator does not say what each side wanted, only who stood where.

a: the Stone of Zoheleth, next to En-rogel
p: En-rogel was a spring in the Kidron valley south of the city, within earshot of Gihon.
b: En-rogel ("spring of the fuller" or "of the foot") was on the border of Judah and Benjamin (Joshua 15:7; Joshua 18:16), usually placed at Bir Ayyub, where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet, south of the City of David. Zoheleth may mean "the creeping one," so "the Serpent's Stone," perhaps an old sacred stone. A sacrificial meal at a holy place was a normal way to proclaim a king (1 Samuel 11:15; 2 Samuel 15:12). Gihon, where Solomon is anointed (1:38), lies about half a mile (800 meters) up the same valley, close enough for Adonijah's guests to hear the shouting (1:41).

a: Adonijah son of Haggith is king now
p: The Hebrew malakh can mean "has become king" or "is acting as king." The text never shows Adonijah crowned.
b: Nathan says malakh Adoniyyahu, "Adonijah reigns" or "has become king." The narrator has told us only that Adonijah said he would be king and held a feast. Whether he had been anointed, or Nathan is making the danger sound worse than it was, the text does not say. Bathsheba repeats it (1:18), and Nathan adds the guests' cry, "Long live King Adonijah!" (1:25), a detail the narrator had not given.

a: you swore an oath to your servant, didn't you?
p: No earlier verse records this oath. Readers have long asked whether Nathan reminded David of a promise or planted one.
b: Nothing in 2 Samuel records David swearing that Solomon would reign. Nathan puts the words in Bathsheba's mouth as a question, then comes in to "make her words complete" (1:14). Many critical and literary readers (R. N. Whybray, Robert Alter, Jerome Walsh) see a court intrigue in which a weak old king is persuaded he made a promise. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers answer that the narrator often tells us things only when they matter, that the LORD had already loved the child and named him through Nathan (2 Samuel 12:24–25), and that Chronicles says God told David that Solomon would build his house and sit on his throne (1 Chronicles 22:9–10; 1 Chronicles 28:5). On either reading, David himself swears to it now (1:30). See the chapter page.

a: make your words complete
p: Nathan will "fill up" Bathsheba's words: confirm them and add to them.
b: The verb is mille', "fill." In 1:14 it can mean to confirm ("fulfill") her words or to complete them with details she leaves out. Nathan does both: he adds the guest list and the shouting (1:25–26). Kings uses the same verb when the LORD "fills" or fulfills his word (2:27; 8:15, 8:24), so the reader may hear a small irony in it.

a: Abishag the Shunammite was waiting on him
p: The narrator places the young Abishag in the room as Bathsheba comes in.
b: The detail is easy to pass over. Bathsheba, who once was the woman David could not stay away from (2 Samuel 11:2–4), now comes to an old man in bed and finds a young woman caring for him. Robert Alter and others hear in the line the passing of time and power. The narrator gives no comment.

a: the LORD your God
p: "The LORD" in small capitals stands for God's personal name, YHWH.
b: As in most English Bibles, "the LORD" in capitals stands for the four Hebrew letters YHWH, God's personal name, which Jews do not say aloud and read as Adonai, "my Lord." Where the Hebrew has Adonai itself, this translation has "the Lord" (3:10), and where it has Adonai YHWH, "the Lord GOD" (2:26; 8:53). See the topic on the names of God.

a: you do not know it
p: The Hebrew says "and now" twice; many manuscripts read the second as "and you."
b: The Hebrew begins the verse with we'attah, "and now," spelled with the letter ayin, and uses the same word again before "my lord the king." Many Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient versions read the second one with the letter aleph, which makes it we'attah, "and you," and fits the verb "you do not know." The two words sound alike. See the variant.

a: all Israel is watching you, waiting for you to tell them who will sit on my lord the king's throne
p: Israel had no fixed rule that the oldest son became king. The king named his heir.
b: In ancient Israel the oldest son had a natural claim, but there was no law that settled it, and kings could choose a younger son (2 Chronicles 11:21–22). Other ancient Near Eastern kings did the same: the Assyrian king Esarhaddon was a younger son chosen over his brothers, and he had to fight for the throne. Bathsheba appeals to this royal right to decide. Later kings of Judah often named a son as co-ruler before they died.

a: my son Solomon and I will be the ones held guilty
p: The word chatta'im, "sinners," here means people counted as offenders, enemies of the new king.
b: Chatta'im usually means "sinners," but its root sense is "miss the mark," and here it means people who will be treated as guilty: rivals to be removed. That fear was real. New rulers in Israel often killed a rival's family (15:29; 16:11; Judges 9:5; 2 Kings 10:11), and Solomon himself will remove Adonijah (2:25).

a: Long live King Adonijah!
p: The shout yechi hammelekh is the cry that greeted a new king.
b: Yechi hammelekh, "may the king live," is the cry of acclamation the people raised for Saul (1 Samuel 10:24), the one Hushai used to fool Absalom (2 Samuel 16:16), and the one that will ring out at Gihon for Solomon (1:34, 1:39). Nathan's report that the guests had shouted it for Adonijah is what makes the feast an act of rebellion.

a: As the LORD lives, who has set my life free from every trouble
p: David uses the same words he once spoke over the murderers of Ish-bosheth.
b: These are almost the words David spoke long before: "As the LORD lives, who has set my life free from every kind of trouble" (2 Samuel 4:9). The verb padah means to ransom or rescue. The old king looks back over a life of danger, from Saul's spears to Absalom's revolt, and credits the LORD with bringing him through it.

a: Put my son Solomon on the mule that is mine
p: Riding the king's own mule told every watcher that David had chosen Solomon.
b: Mules were the mounts of David's sons (2 Samuel 13:29; 2 Samuel 18:9). Since the law forbade breeding two kinds of animals together (Leviticus 19:19), mules were probably imported, and costly (10:25). Putting Solomon on the king's own mule was a public sign anyone could read, like the robe and ring Pharaoh gave Joseph (Genesis 41:42–43). The rabbis taught that no one else may ride a king's animal (Mishnah Sanhedrin 2:5). Christian readers have compared Jesus riding into Jerusalem on a donkey as the son of David (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:1–9).
r: 2 Samuel 13:29; 2 Samuel 18:9; Leviticus 19:19; 10:25; Genesis 41:42–43; Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:1–9

a: Gihon
p: Gihon was Jerusalem's main spring, below the City of David on its east side.
b: The Gihon ("gusher") spring rises in the Kidron valley at the foot of the City of David. It was the city's water supply, and later King Hezekiah cut a tunnel to bring its water inside the walls (2 Chronicles 32:30; 2 Kings 20:20). A great tower and pool built around the spring in the Middle Bronze Age have been excavated by Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron, though radiocarbon dates published in 2017 suggest that parts of it are much later, perhaps late 9th century BC, and the date is now debated. The name is the same as one of the rivers of Eden (Genesis 2:13); some readers see a deliberate link between the garden and the city of the temple.

a: Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet will anoint him there as king
p: Saul and David were anointed by a prophet; Solomon is anointed by a priest, with a prophet beside him.
b: Samuel the prophet anointed Saul and David in private (1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Samuel 16:13); David was then anointed in public by the people of Judah and the elders of Israel (2 Samuel 2:4; 2 Samuel 5:3). Here David orders a public anointing by priest and prophet together, and 1:39 says Zadok did it. Anointing with oil set a person apart for God's service and made the king "the LORD's anointed," meshiach YHWH, the word that later became "Messiah." Hittite and Egyptian texts also describe anointing officials and vassal kings.
r: 1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Samuel 16:13; 2 Samuel 2:4; 2 Samuel 5:3; 1:39; 2 Kings 9:6; 2 Kings 11:12

a: ruler over Israel and over Judah
p: Nagid, "ruler," is the word used for Saul and David as God's chosen leaders. "Israel and Judah" hints at a union of two parts.
b: David names Solomon nagid, "ruler," the title God's prophets gave Saul and David (1 Samuel 9:16; 1 Samuel 13:14; 2 Samuel 5:2). Here the king himself uses it. He also names the two parts of the kingdom separately: Judah, which had first made David king at Hebron, and Israel, the northern tribes who joined him later (2 Samuel 2:4; 5:1–3). The union will last only through Solomon's reign (12:16–20).

a: Amen!
p: Amen means "so be it," "it is sure." Benaiah adds a prayer that the LORD will agree.
b: Amen comes from the root for firmness and trust (the same root as emunah, "faithfulness"). It is the people's answer to a curse or blessing (Deuteronomy 27:15–26; Nehemiah 8:6). Benaiah, the commander of the guard, says it first, then asks that the LORD himself "say so": a royal command needs God's yes to stand.

a: the Kerethites and the Pelethites
p: These were David's professional bodyguard, probably men from Crete and from the Philistines.
b: The Kerethites were probably Cretans; the Negev near Philistia had a "Kerethite" district (1 Samuel 30:14; Zephaniah 2:5). The Pelethites are usually taken as Philistines. Under Benaiah they were the king's personal troops (2 Samuel 8:18; 2 Samuel 20:23), loyal to the king rather than to any tribe. Their presence at Gihon meant that the army in Jerusalem was with Solomon, whatever Joab did.

a: From the tent Zadok the priest took the horn of oil
p: The tent is the one David set up for the ark in Jerusalem; the horn held the holy anointing oil.
b: David had brought the ark into Jerusalem and placed it "within the tent that David had set up for it" (2 Samuel 6:17). The holy anointing oil was kept there, in a ram's horn like the one Samuel used (1 Samuel 16:13). Exodus gives the recipe of the sacred oil and forbids its use for ordinary purposes (Exodus 30:22–33). The rabbis held that a king's son who came to the throne without a dispute was not anointed, and that Solomon was anointed because of Adonijah's challenge (Bavli Horayot 11b).

a: the noise they made split the earth
p: The verb means "split." It is a bold picture of a deafening roar.
b: Wattibbaqa' ha'arets means "the earth split open," the verb used when the ground swallowed Korah (Numbers 16:31). Here it is joyful exaggeration. The Greek has "the earth resounded" (ēchēsen hē gē), and some scholars change a letter or two of the Hebrew to match it, but no Hebrew manuscript reads so. English idiom would say the noise was deafening.

a: Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest
p: Jonathan had carried secret news for David during Absalom's revolt.
b: Jonathan and Ahimaaz, the sons of the two priests, were David's messengers when he fled Absalom (2 Samuel 15:27, 15:36; 2 Samuel 17:17–21). Now Jonathan carries news against his own father's side. Adonijah's greeting, "You are a man of worth, so your news is good," sounds like David's words about Ahimaaz (2 Samuel 18:27). Both times the hope is wrong.

a: the king bowed down there on his bed
p: Like Jacob at the end of his life, the old king bows on his bed.
b: The scene recalls Jacob, who made Joseph swear to bury him in the promised land, "And Israel bowed down at the head of the bed" (Genesis 47:31). Both old men see the future of God's promise settled before they die. David's bow is worship: he gives thanks that he has lived to see his heir on the throne (1:48).

a: took hold of the horns of the altar
p: The altar was a place of refuge, but the law did not protect a deliberate killer there.
b: The horns were the raised corners of an altar; several stone altars with horns have been found, such as the large horned altar from Beersheba. A person in danger could seize them and claim God's protection. But the law limits that safety: "if someone schemes against his neighbor to kill him by a trick, take him away even from my altar to die" (Exodus 21:14). Adonijah is spared (1:53); Joab, who had murdered two men, is not (2:28–34).

a: not a single hair of his will fall to the ground
p: A set phrase for complete safety, used by Saul's soldiers and by David.
b: The people used it to save Jonathan: "not a single hair from his head will drop to the ground" (1 Samuel 14:45), and David to the wise woman of Tekoa (2 Samuel 14:11). Solomon's version comes with a condition: if Adonijah proves to be a "man of worth." A similar phrase, ish chayil, was Adonijah's word for Jonathan (1:42). Jesus uses the image for God's care (Luke 21:18).

a: "Go home," Solomon told him
p: Solomon spares his brother, but on terms. Readers differ on how generous this is.
b: Some readers see real mercy: Solomon begins his reign without bloodshed, as Saul once did (1 Samuel 11:13). Others note that "Go home" keeps Adonijah away from court and on probation, and that Solomon has already left himself a way to kill him (1:52). Both may be true. The test comes quickly (2:13–25).

a: I am going the way of all the earth
p: David's farewell follows the pattern of Moses' and Joshua's last charges.
b: Joshua used the same words: "Look, today I am going the way of all the earth" (Joshua 23:14). Like Moses to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:7, 31:23) and Joshua to Israel, David tells his successor to be strong and keep the law. The model of a dying leader's charge shapes the first half of David's speech (2:2–4); the second half (2:5–9) is very different.

a: Be a man
p: Literally "become a man": grow up, act with courage.
b: Wehayita le'ish means "become a man." The Philistines urged one another in the same way before battle (1 Samuel 4:9). Jewish tradition took it to mean that Solomon was very young (see the note on 3:7). The phrase calls for courage and maturity, not for harshness, though harsh tasks follow.

a: just as they are written in the law of Moses
p: This verse is a string of Deuteronomy's phrases. Most scholars see the hand of the book's editors.
b: "Walk in his ways," "his rules, his commands, his rulings and his decrees," "the law of Moses" and "act wisely" are all the vocabulary of Deuteronomy and Joshua (Deuteronomy 8:6; 11:1; Joshua 1:7–8). Critical scholars, following Martin Noth, take 2:3–4 as part of the Deuteronomistic History's framework, setting out the standard by which every king will be judged. Traditional readers answer that David, who knew the law, could have spoken this way. The word torah means "instruction" or "teaching" as well as "law." See also Joshua 1:7: "so that you will act wisely wherever you go."

a: If your sons guard their way
p: God's promise to David in 2 Samuel 7 had no "if." Here, and in 8:25 and 9:4–5, it has one.
b: In 2 Samuel 7 God promises that David's throne will stand firm "for all time" and that a guilty son will be corrected but not rejected (2 Samuel 7:14–16). Kings repeats the promise with a condition: "if your sons guard their way." Readers explain this in several ways. Some see two layers of editing, an older unconditional promise and a later conditional one written after the exile (Frank Moore Cross). Others hold that the two belong together: the dynasty itself is promised, but each king's share in it depends on loyalty (Psalm 89:30–37; Psalm 132:11–12). Christians read the unconditional promise as kept in Jesus, the son of David (Luke 1:32–33).

a: In time of peace he spilled blood as if at war
p: Is David seeking justice for murders, or settling scores? Readers have long disagreed.
b: Joab murdered Abner (2 Samuel 3:27) and Amasa (2 Samuel 20:10) in peacetime, by treachery. David cursed him but never punished him (2 Samuel 3:28–39). One reading (many traditional and some modern commentators) sees a dying king trying to lift blood guilt from his house, as the law required: blood shed in the land had to be answered (Numbers 35:33). Another sees cold politics: Joab had backed Adonijah and was dangerous, and David uses old crimes to get rid of him. Notice that David does not mention Joab's killing of Absalom (2 Samuel 18:14), and that "what Joab ... did to me" puts David's own honor first. The Talmud weighs Joab's loyalty and his crimes against each other (Bavli Sanhedrin 49a). See the chapter page.

a: on the belt at his waist and on the sandals on his feet
p: The blood on Joab's belt and sandals is a picture of guilt that clings to him.
b: When Joab stabbed Amasa, his sword was fastened in its sheath at his belt (2 Samuel 20:8). Blood on the belt and sandals pictures a man covered in guilt from waist to feet. Some scholars, such as John Gray, think the phrase also points at David: Joab's murders stained the king who failed to punish them. That reading draws on the Lucianic Greek and Old Latin, which have "my belt ... my sandals," with David speaking; see the variant.

a: Amasa son of Jether
p: 2 Samuel 17:25 calls Amasa's father Ithra; here and in 1 Chronicles 2:17 he is Jether.
b: The Hebrew spells the name Yeter here and in 2:32, and Yitra in 2 Samuel 17:25, where the site's Plain has "Ithra the Israelite." 1 Chronicles 2:17 has Jether and calls him an Ishmaelite, which many scholars think is the original reading in Samuel too. The two names are forms of one name.

a: Sheol
p: Sheol is the Hebrew name for the world of the dead, the grave.
b: She'ol is where all the dead go, good and bad (Genesis 37:35; Psalm 89:48). To go down to Sheol "in peace" was to die old and at rest. David asks that Joab's gray head not go down that way. The King James Version renders She'ol as "the grave" here and "hell" in some other places; the Hebrew word does not mean a place of punishment.

a: you must show loyal love
p: Hesed, "loyal love," is faithful kindness that keeps a bond, here a debt of gratitude.
b: Hesed is the love that keeps faith within a relationship. Barzillai had fed David's army at Mahanaim during Absalom's revolt (2 Samuel 17:27–29; 2 Samuel 19:31–39), and David had asked him to come to court; the old man sent his son Chimham instead. To "eat from the king's table" was a royal pension, as for Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:7). The same word describes God's loyal love to David (3:6; 8:23).

a: I gave him my oath by the LORD: 'I will not kill you with the sword.'
p: David swore not to kill Shimei, then tells Solomon to make sure he dies. Was that faithful to the oath?
b: Shimei cursed David as he fled Jerusalem (2 Samuel 16:5–13) and later begged forgiveness (2 Samuel 19:16–23), and David told him, "You will not die," and gave him his oath on it (2 Samuel 19:23). Some readers say David kept his word: he never harmed Shimei, and the oath did not bind his son. Others say this keeps the letter of the oath and breaks its spirit. A curse against the king was a crime under the law (Exodus 22:28), and some think David feared the curse itself would harm his house until it was answered. The narrator gives no verdict, and Solomon in the end gives Shimei a chance (2:36–38).

a: they buried him in the City of David
p: David was buried inside his city. Peter later says his tomb was still known.
b: Burial inside a city was unusual and a mark of royal honor; most kings of Judah were later buried there too (11:43; 14:31). Peter could say in Jerusalem, "his tomb is with us to this day" (Acts 2:29), and Josephus reports that Hyrcanus and Herod robbed it of treasure (Antiquities 7.392–394). The site now shown as "David's Tomb" on the western hill called Mount Zion is a medieval tradition; the real City of David lies on the eastern ridge.

a: He reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem
p: David's forty years are a round total; 2 Samuel 5:5 gives seven and a half years in Hebron.
b: 2 Samuel 5:5 says David ruled Judah in Hebron for "seven years and six months." Here the total is rounded to forty. Forty is also the length given for Saul (Acts 13:21) and Solomon (11:42), and some scholars think it is a stock figure for a full generation. Most date David's reign to about 1010–970 BC. This verse ends the section of the Greek Bible revised by the kaige editors; see the variant at 1:8.

a: Solomon sat on the throne of David his father, and his kingdom grew very secure
p: This line and 2:46 frame the story of how Solomon's kingdom was made secure.
b: Chapter 2 is bracketed: "his kingdom grew very secure" (2:12) and "the kingdom was firm in Solomon's hand" (2:46). Between them come three deaths and a banishment. The frame tells the reader what the purge was for. A Jewish tradition, recorded in the chronicle Seder Olam and followed by Rashi, holds that Solomon was only twelve when he became king; most modern scholars think he was about twenty.

a: Is it peace that brings you?
p: Bathsheba's question shows she is wary of Adonijah.
b: The question echoes the elders of Bethlehem, shaking as Samuel arrived: "Have you come in peace?" (1 Samuel 16:4). Shalom, "peace," is the theme of Solomon's reign, and Solomon's name (Shelomoh) sounds like it. Here the word hides fear.

a: for it came to him from the LORD
p: Adonijah admits God gave the kingship to Solomon, even as he insists it was really his.
b: Adonijah's words carry both a complaint and an admission. "All Israel had set their faces toward me" claims popular support, and "the kingship belonged to me" claims the right of the oldest. Yet he says that Solomon's rule came "from the LORD." Some readers hear sincere resignation; others hear a man saying what is safe while he plans his next move. The narrator lets the request that follows decide.

a: Let him give me Abishag the Shunammite to be my wife
p: Taking a dead king's woman could signal a claim to his throne. Was Adonijah's request a plot or a love match?
b: In Israel a man who took the women of the king's household made a claim on the king's place: Absalom did it to his father's concubines (2 Samuel 16:21–22), Ish-bosheth feared it of Abner (2 Samuel 3:7), and God gave Saul's wives to David (2 Samuel 12:8). Many readers agree with Solomon that Adonijah's request was a quiet bid for the throne (2:22). Others point out that Abishag was never David's wife or concubine (1:4), that Adonijah asked openly through the queen mother, and that he may simply have wanted her; on this view Solomon used the request as an excuse. The rabbis also differ. The narrator reports only the words and the result.

a: a throne was set out for the king's mother. She sat at his right
p: The king's mother held an honored office at court, the gevirah or "great lady."
b: In Judah the king's mother had a title, gevirah, "great lady" (15:13; Jeremiah 13:18), and Kings names the mother of almost every king of Judah (14:21; 15:2). Her seat at the king's right hand was the place of highest honor (Psalm 110:1; Psalm 45:9). Solomon bows to Bathsheba, as she had bowed to David (1:16). Catholic and Orthodox writers have seen in this scene a picture of Mary, the mother of the Son of David, honored as queen mother; Protestant readers generally do not draw that link.

a: God do this to me, and more besides
p: A standard oath: the speaker calls down harm on himself if he does not keep his word.
b: The full formula, "So may God do to me and so may he add," probably went with a gesture, such as a cut animal (Genesis 15:9–17; Jeremiah 34:18). Ruth (Ruth 1:17), Saul (1 Samuel 14:44) and David (2 Samuel 3:35) all use it. Solomon swears by it that Adonijah has spoken "at the cost of his life."
orig: כֹּה יַעֲשֶׂה־לִּי אֱלֹהִים וְכֹה יוֹסִיף (koh ya'aseh-li Elohim wekhoh yosif)

a: who has made me a house just as he said he would
p: Solomon claims the promise of 2 Samuel 7: "the LORD will make a house for you."
b: Nathan had told David, "the LORD will make a house for you" (2 Samuel 7:11), meaning a dynasty. Solomon claims that promise as his own, and so makes the killing of a rival part of keeping God's word. Some readers find this troubling; others say a king had to protect the line God promised.

a: Benaiah fell on Adonijah, and Adonijah died
p: Was Adonijah's execution justice for a renewed plot, or the removal of a rival?
b: Traditional readers, Jewish and Christian, have mostly accepted Solomon's judgment: Adonijah had tried to seize the throne once, broke the terms on which he was spared (1:52), and the request for Abishag showed he had not given up. Many modern readers see a ruthless purge, of a kind well known in the ancient world: an Assyrian or Persian king who came to the throne over his brothers often killed them. Some, such as Walter Brueggemann, read the narrator as quietly critical of Solomon. Others, like Iain Provan, see a narrator who shows both God's purpose and human ruthlessness without excusing either. To "fall on" someone is Hebrew for attacking and killing.

a: Off to Anathoth, to your own fields!
p: Abiathar was banished to Anathoth, a priests' town north of Jerusalem. Jeremiah later came from there.
b: Anathoth (modern Anata, near Ras el-Kharrubeh) was one of the towns given to the priests in Benjamin (Joshua 21:18). Three centuries later the prophet Jeremiah was "from the priests who were in Anathoth" (Jeremiah 1:1), and many scholars think he descended from Abiathar's family. If so, the last priest of Eli's house to serve in Jerusalem had a descendant who preached against its temple (Jeremiah 7:12–14).

a: the word he had spoken in Shiloh against Eli's family
p: Abiathar's removal fulfills the prophecy against Eli's house given at Shiloh.
b: A man of God had told Eli that his family would lose the priesthood and that God would "raise up a faithful priest" (1 Samuel 2:35), and the LORD repeated it to young Samuel (1 Samuel 3:11–14). Abiathar was the great-great-grandson of Eli (1 Samuel 14:3; 1 Samuel 22:20). Kings often notes such fulfillments; it is one of its ways of showing that God's word directs history (see 8:15, 8:24).

a: So Joab ran to the LORD's tent and grabbed the horns of the altar
p: Solomon has Joab killed at the altar. Was this a just sentence for murder, or a political killing?
b: Joab had committed two murders (2:5, 2:32), and the law says such a killer may be taken even from the altar (Exodus 21:14). On this reading, Solomon finally does what David failed to do, and removes the guilt of innocent blood from the land (2:31–33). On a political reading, Joab dies because he backed Adonijah, as the narrator's own remark in this verse hints, and the old murders give a legal cover. Josephus and many rabbis took the first view; many modern historians the second. Notice that Joab, unlike Adonijah, does not ask for mercy, and that Benaiah hesitates to kill a man at the altar (2:30).

a: Here is where I will die
t: Why Joab will not come out
p: Joab may hope to shame Solomon, or to die at a holy place, or to win burial with honor.
b: Readers have offered several reasons. Joab may hope that Solomon will not dare to shed blood at the altar. He may want to die at the sanctuary rather than as a common criminal. The Talmud imagines Joab reasoning that if the king had him killed his property would go to the crown, but if he died by sentence of a court it would go to his heirs (Bavli Sanhedrin 48b). Solomon calls the bluff: he grants Joab's wish to die there, and also grants him burial (2:31, 2:34).

a: his throne will have peace from the LORD
p: The word shalom plays on the name Solomon, Shelomoh.
b: Solomon's name, Shelomoh, sounds like shalom, "peace," and 1 Chronicles 22:9 makes the link plain: "Solomon will be his name, and in his days I will give Israel peace and calm." In chapter 2 the word comes again and again: Joab shed blood "in peace" (2:5), his gray hair must not go down "in peace" (2:6), Adonijah comes "in peace" (2:13), and now peace is promised to David's throne. The peace of Solomon's reign begins with blood.

a: In Abiathar's place he put Zadok the priest
p: From here on Zadok's line holds the high priesthood in Jerusalem until the 2nd century BC.
b: Chronicles traces Zadok to Aaron through Eleazar (1 Chronicles 6:4–8), while Abiathar's line came through Eli. Some scholars, such as H. H. Rowley, have argued that Zadok was a Jebusite priest of Jerusalem taken over by David; most now treat this as possible but unproven. Ezekiel later limits priestly service to "the sons of Zadok" (Ezekiel 44:15), and the Dead Sea Scrolls community called its priests "sons of Zadok." The Sadducees' name probably comes from Zadok as well.

a: cross the Kidron Valley
p: The Kidron lies east of Jerusalem, on the road to Shimei's home at Bahurim.
b: Bahurim, Shimei's town, lay east of Jerusalem beyond the Mount of Olives (2 Samuel 16:5), so the Kidron was the line he would cross to go home and stir up trouble among Saul's clan. When Shimei later goes to Gath, he travels west or southwest and may not have crossed the Kidron at all. Solomon's later charge says only "go out and travel here or there" (2:42). The point was that Shimei had left the city, not which valley he crossed.

a: Achish son of Maacah, the king of Gath
p: A king named Achish had sheltered David some forty years earlier.
b: David had served "Achish son of Maoch, the king of Gath" (1 Samuel 27:2). Maoch and Maacah may be the same name, and the king may be the same man after forty years, or a grandson with the same name. An inscription found at Ekron names a later Philistine ruler Ikausu (Achish), so the name was in use among Philistine kings. Gath (Tell es-Safi) was a large Philistine city, excavated by Aren Maeir.

a: the throne of David will stand firm in the LORD's presence for all time
p: Solomon answers Shimei's old curse with God's promise to David.
b: Shimei had cursed David (2 Samuel 16:7–8). Solomon sets that curse against God's promise that David's throne would stand firm for all time (2 Samuel 7:16), and turns the harm back on the one who spoke it. The king who is blessed and the curse that returns on its speaker recall God's word to Abraham: "whoever treats you with contempt I will curse" (Genesis 12:3).

a: Solomon became Pharaoh's son-in-law
p: A marriage into Egypt's royal house was a mark of high rank. Kings mentions it five times.
b: The verb hitchatten means to become someone's in-law by marriage, a political alliance. In an Egyptian-era letter of the 14th century BC, a Babylonian king complains that Pharaoh Amenhotep III refused him a princess, saying that no daughter of the king of Egypt had ever been given to anyone (Amarna letter EA 4). By Solomon's time Egypt was weaker, and the gift of Gezer as a dowry (9:16) fits a Pharaoh of the 21st dynasty, perhaps Siamun, who raided Philistia. Kings returns to this wife again and again (7:8; 9:16, 9:24; 11:1). Deuteronomy warns a king against many wives and against leading the people back to Egypt (Deuteronomy 17:16–17), and many readers hear a first quiet warning here.

a: the high places
p: A bamah was a local shrine, often on a hill, with an altar. Kings comes to condemn them.
b: A bamah (plural bamot) was a raised place of worship, often outdoors, with an altar and sometimes a standing stone. Samuel had offered sacrifice at one (1 Samuel 9:12–14). The narrator excuses the people for using them "up to that time," because the house for the LORD's name was not yet built (Deuteronomy 12:10–14). After the temple stands, Kings judges every king by whether he removed the high places (15:14; 2 Kings 18:4; 2 Kings 23:8).

a: Only, he too sacrificed at the high places
p: The little word raq, "only," comes twice in two verses. Readers debate whether it is a criticism.
b: Raq, "only, except," begins 3:2 and comes again in 3:3. Solomon loved the LORD, the narrator says, "only" he worshiped at the high places. Some readers, such as Jerome Walsh and Iain Provan, hear the first crack in a portrait that will end with Solomon building high places for foreign gods (11:7). Others think the remark is simply an explanation of why he went to Gibeon. Kings says of no other king that he "loved the LORD," the very thing Deuteronomy 6:5 commands.

a: The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice, since the greatest high place was there
p: Gibeon, six miles northwest of Jerusalem, had the leading shrine of the time.
b: Gibeon (el-Jib) is about 6 miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem. Chronicles explains why it was "the greatest": the tabernacle, the tent of meeting that Moses had made in the wilderness, stood there, with the bronze altar (2 Chronicles 1:3–6; 1 Chronicles 16:39). Kings does not say this. Excavations at el-Jib by James Pritchard in 1956–1962 found a great rock-cut pool and jar handles inscribed with the name "Gibeon" (gb'n).

a: in a dream in the night, that the LORD showed himself to Solomon
t: Kings who dream at a shrine
p: Ancient kings told of dreams at holy places in which a god promised them the throne. Solomon's dream fits that pattern, with a difference.
b: Egyptian and Mesopotamian kings recorded dreams in which a god spoke to them, often at a shrine. The best known is the "Dream Stele" of Thutmose IV, which says the god spoke to him in his sleep under the Sphinx and promised him the kingdom. A Sumerian ruler, Gudea of Lagash, was shown in a dream how to build his god's temple. Many scholars therefore call 3:4–15 a royal dream report and compare its form to these. The difference is in the content: Solomon is not simply promised power; he is asked what he wants and chooses the wisdom to judge. On dreams in the Bible see Genesis 28:12–17 and Genesis 41.

a: in truth and in what was right, with an honest heart
p: Solomon praises David's honesty and right living. The reader of 2 Samuel knows a more complicated story.
b: Kings regularly holds David up as the model king, the one whose "heart was whole" with the LORD (11:4; 15:3–5). 15:5 adds an exception, "except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite." Readers take this in different ways: as forgiveness, which no longer counts the sin (Psalm 32:1–2); as idealizing, which forgets it; or as a standard of loyalty to the LORD alone, which David, unlike later kings, never broke by worshiping other gods.

a: I am only a youngster
p: Solomon calls himself a na'ar qaton, "a little boy." It is humility more than a statement of age.
b: Na'ar qaton literally means "a small boy." Jeremiah uses na'ar of himself when he protests his call (Jeremiah 1:6). Solomon had a son, Rehoboam, born about a year before he became king (14:21 with 11:42), so he was a young man, not a child; most estimates put him around twenty. Jewish tradition (Rashi, following Seder Olam) says twelve. Either way, the phrase is the language of a humble prayer, not a birth certificate.

a: a heart that listens
p: The Hebrew lev shomea' is "a hearing heart." Many Bibles say "an understanding mind," which loses the picture of listening.
b: Solomon asks for a lev shomea', literally "a heart that hears." In Hebrew the heart is the seat of thought and will, not only of feeling, so some translations say "mind" or "understanding." But the verb shama' is "hear, listen, obey," the first word of the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), and it matters: a judge must listen to both sides, and a king must listen to God. God's answer picks up the word: Solomon asked "to hear cases" (3:11), and the two women's story that follows is a test of listening.

a: see the difference between good and bad
p: The phrase recalls the tree of the knowledge of good and evil and the wise woman's praise of David.
b: The wise woman of Tekoa told David that he was "like God's angel at hearing out good and evil" (2 Samuel 14:17). The phrase can mean the whole range of things, or right and wrong in a court case. Many readers also hear Genesis 2–3: the first humans grabbed at knowing good and evil, while Solomon asks for it as a gift so that he can serve. When he later turns from God (chapter 11), the comparison sharpens.

a: The Lord liked what Solomon had asked for
p: Here the Hebrew has Adonai, "Lord," not the name YHWH.
b: Most of this chapter uses the name YHWH, but this verse has Adonai, "the Lord." Some Hebrew manuscripts read YHWH here. The change may only be variety, or the rabbis' habit of reading Adonai for YHWH may have crept into the written text. See the note on 1:17.

a: You did not ask to live many days
p: Solomon did not ask for long life, riches or revenge, and God gives him more than he asked.
b: Long life, wealth and victory over enemies were what ancient kings usually asked of their gods; Psalm 21:4 and Psalm 72 pray for them for Israel's king. Solomon's choice and God's answer have been read by Christians alongside Jesus' words, "Seek God's kingdom and his righteousness before anything else, and you will receive all these things in addition" (Matthew 6:33), and James's promise that God gives wisdom to anyone who asks (James 1:5). Jewish readers have drawn the same lesson from Proverbs 3:13–16, where wisdom holds long life in one hand and riches and honor in the other.

a: No one before you was your equal, and no one after you will rise up to equal you
p: Kings says this kind of thing about three kings: Solomon for wisdom, Hezekiah for trust, Josiah for keeping the law.
b: The same pattern of praise is used of Hezekiah, who trusted the LORD more than any king before or after him (2 Kings 18:5), and of Josiah, who kept the law of Moses like no king before or after (2 Kings 23:25). Each is unique in a different gift. Readers who press the words as a strict claim notice that they cannot all be literally true at once; most take them as the high praise of a royal record.

a: riches and glory
p: Kavod means weight, wealth and honor. It is also the word for the LORD's glory in 8:11.
b: Kavod comes from the root "heavy." A person of kavod carries weight: wealth, reputation, honor. The same word is used for the LORD's glory that fills the temple (8:11). The chapters that follow show Solomon's kavod on display (4:20–34; 10:1–29).

a: If you walk in my ways
p: The gift of wisdom and riches is free, but long life is promised on a condition.
b: God gives wisdom, riches and glory without a condition, but long life only "if you walk in my ways." Solomon reigned forty years (11:42), and if he became king at about twenty he died near sixty, ten years short of David's seventy (2 Samuel 5:4). Many readers connect this with his later turning away (11:4–11).

a: Solomon woke up. It had been a dream!
p: The same words close Pharaoh's dream in Joseph's story.
b: The Hebrew wehinneh chalom, "and look, a dream," is the phrase used when Pharaoh wakes in Genesis: "Pharaoh woke, and there it was: a dream" (Genesis 41:7). In both stories a king receives a dream from God, and in both wisdom follows. Solomon goes at once from Gibeon to the ark in Jerusalem, as if to give the place of the ark first honor.

a: They were prostitutes
p: The Hebrew zonot means prostitutes. The Aramaic Targum makes them "innkeepers," as it did for Rahab.
b: Zonot is the plain word for prostitutes. That they could bring their case to the king shows that the lowest in society had a right to his justice (Psalm 72:4). It also explains why there were no husbands or witnesses in the story. The Aramaic Targum Jonathan, which often softens such details, calls them "innkeepers," the word it also uses for Rahab (Joshua 2:1).

a: Later two women came to the king
t: The two mothers around the world
p: Stories of a judge who finds a child's true mother by a test are told in India, China and elsewhere. Who borrowed from whom is unknown.
b: Hugo Gressmann collected more than twenty versions of this tale in 1907. In an Indian Buddhist story (the Mahosadha Jataka), a wise judge draws a line and has two women pull the child across it; the true mother lets go rather than hurt him. A Chinese drama of the 13th century, The Chalk Circle, uses the same test, and Bertolt Brecht turned it into The Caucasian Chalk Circle (1944), where the woman who raised the child, not the birth mother, wins. Most scholars think the story was a widespread folk motif. The biblical version is the oldest written one known, but that does not prove the others came from it. Its point is its own: the king's wisdom from God finds the truth when there are no witnesses.

a: No outsider was with us in the house; only the two of us were there
p: Ancient law needed two witnesses. Here there are none, and the king must find the truth another way.
b: The law required two or three witnesses for a conviction (Deuteronomy 19:15). The first woman is careful to explain why she has none. Her story, though detailed, is also something she could not know: she was asleep when the switch was made (3:20). The case is a classic test of a judge with no evidence but the claims of the two parties.

a: felt her love for her son burning inside her
p: Rachamim, "compassion," comes from rechem, "womb." Her womb-love "grew hot."
b: The Hebrew says nikhmeru rachameha, "her compassions grew warm." Rachamim is from the word for womb, and its sense is the tender love a mother has for the child she bore. Joseph's heart "grew warm" in the same way for his brother Benjamin (Genesis 43:30). The same word is often used for God's compassion (Isaiah 49:15; Psalm 103:13). Solomon's test works because he knows this love would rather lose the child than see him die.

a: Give the live child to her
p: "To her" is unclear in Hebrew. The king is pointing to the woman who begged for the child's life.
b: The Hebrew simply says "give her the live child," repeating the words of the true mother in 3:26, "give her the live child." The king turns her plea back to her. The Greek translators made it explicit: "give it to the one who said, 'Give it to her.'" The narrator never tells us which woman spoke first in 3:17, so the reader, like the king, learns the truth only from the test.

a: God's wisdom was in him for doing justice
p: For the Bible, the first use of a king's wisdom is justice for the weak.
b: The people "feared" the king, in the sense of awe and respect. The chapter's point is that God's wisdom (chokhmat Elohim) is given to do mishpat, justice. Psalm 72, "of Solomon," prays the same: "God, give your rulings to the king" (Psalm 72:1), and "rulings" is the same word, mishpat. Isaiah describes the coming son of Jesse with the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, who will judge the poor with justice (Isaiah 11:2–4).

a: the priest, Azariah son of Zadok
p: The list of officials shows a court grown larger than David's.
b: David's lists of officials (2 Samuel 8:16–18; 2 Samuel 20:23–26) name an army commander, a recorder, priests, a scribe and the head of the guard. Solomon's adds new offices: a head of the district officers, a palace manager, and the "king's friend." Azariah is probably Zadok's grandson, son of Ahimaaz (1 Chronicles 6:8–9); Hebrew "son" can mean descendant. Some scholars (Tryggve Mettinger) see Egyptian models behind some of these offices.

a: sons of Shisha
p: Shisha may be the same man as David's scribe Seraiah, Shavsha or Sheva, possibly an Egyptian name or title.
b: David's scribe is called Seraiah (2 Samuel 8:17), Sheva (2 Samuel 20:25) and Shavsha (1 Chronicles 18:16). Shisha is probably the same man. Some scholars have suggested that these forms reflect an Egyptian title for a royal letter-writer, which would fit a scribal school trained in Egyptian ways; the idea is debated. The "recorder" (mazkir, "one who reminds") was probably the royal herald or keeper of records.

a: priests, Zadok and Abiathar
p: Abiathar had been banished (2:27), yet the list names him. It was probably copied from a record of the early reign.
b: Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood (2:26–27). His name here suggests that the list came from a court document of the first days of the reign, or that Abiathar kept the title in name. Benaiah's place over the army fits after 2:35, so the list may be a mix of times. Lists like this were probably kept in the royal archives the book names (11:41).

a: priest and the king's friend
p: "The king's friend" was a court title for a trusted adviser.
b: Hushai is called "David's friend" (2 Samuel 15:37; 16:16), and Egyptian courts had a similar title. Zabud son of Nathan, perhaps the prophet's son, holds it here. He is also called a priest (kohen), which can mean a royal official as well as a priest at the altar; David's sons were called kohanim too (2 Samuel 8:18).

a: over the palace, Ahishar
p: "Over the house" was a high office, the king's chief steward. A tomb inscription near Jerusalem may name a later holder.
b: The one "over the house" ran the king's estates and household; later holders of the office include Obadiah (18:3), Shebna and Eliakim (Isaiah 22:15–22). A rock-cut tomb in the Silwan village across the Kidron has an inscription of the 8th–7th century BC for "...yahu who is over the house," which some scholars connect with Shebna(yahu). Seal impressions with the same title have also been found.

a: over the forced labor, Adoniram son of Abda
p: Mas was work the state required of its people. Adoniram ran it under three kings and was killed for it.
b: Mas was compulsory labor for the king, a system known across the ancient Near East (Amarna letters from Canaan mention it). Adoniram (Adoram) held the post under David (2 Samuel 20:24), under Solomon, and at the start of Rehoboam's reign, when the northern tribes stoned him to death (12:18). That event shows how hated the system became. See 5:13.

a: Solomon had twelve officers posted over all Israel
p: Each district fed the court for one month. The districts do not follow the old tribal borders exactly.
b: Some districts are named by tribe (Ephraim, Naphtali, Asher, Issachar, Benjamin), others by regions and cities that include old Canaanite towns (4:9, 4:12). Many historians, following Albrecht Alt, see an attempt to bring the Canaanite cities and the tribes under one royal system. Judah is not clearly on the list (see 4:19), and some think it was spared, which would help explain the northern tribes' complaint about Solomon's "heavy yoke" (12:4). Twelve was a natural number for a monthly rota, as in David's army (1 Chronicles 27:1–15).

a: Ben-hur
t: Officers known only by their fathers
p: Five officers are named only as "son of" someone. The list may come from a damaged document.
b: Ben-hur, Ben-deker, Ben-hesed, Ben-abinadab and Ben-geber are given only their fathers' names. One suggestion is that the right-hand edge of a written list, where personal names stood, had broken off. Another is that these were hereditary offices known by family name. Either way it hints that the writer used an older document rather than making the list up.

a: Taanach and Megiddo, and all of Beth-shean
p: These were old Canaanite cities in the Jezreel valley, on the main trade road.
b: Taanach, Megiddo and Beth-shean were cities the tribes had not taken in Joshua's day (Judges 1:27). Placing them under a royal officer shows the new state's reach. All three have been excavated. At Megiddo, a gate and buildings once dated to Solomon are now at the center of a debate about the size of his kingdom; see the topic on the united monarchy debate and 9:15.

a: sixty great towns with walls and bronze bars
p: Argob in Bashan, east of the Jordan, was famous for its many walled towns.
b: Deuteronomy describes the same region: "sixty towns, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan" (Deuteronomy 3:4). The towns of Jair son of Manasseh are named in Numbers 32:41. "Bronze bars" held the gates shut. Ramoth-gilead, the officer's base, will be fought over by Ahab and the Arameans (22:3).

a: And there was one officer
p: The Hebrew is unclear. Many scholars think it refers to Judah, and some Greek manuscripts say so.
b: The Hebrew ends the list with "and one officer who was in the land," without naming the land. The next verse begins with the word "Judah." Many scholars think "Judah" belongs at the end of this verse: "and one officer in the land of Judah," and the Greek supports reading it so (see the variant). If so, Judah had its own officer and was not exempt. If the Hebrew is right as it stands, the "one officer" may be the chief over all the others (4:5) or an officer over the land of Gilead just named.
orig: וּנְצִיב אֶחָד אֲשֶׁר בָּאָרֶץ (unetsiv echad asher ba'arets)

a: like the sand beside the sea in number
p: God's promise to Abraham is pictured as fulfilled in Solomon's day.
b: God had promised Abraham offspring "as many as the stars in the sky and the sand on the seashore" (Genesis 22:17). Eating, drinking and rejoicing is the picture of the good life in God's land (Deuteronomy 12:7; Ecclesiastes 2:24). The narrator presents Solomon's reign as the high point of the promises.

a: Solomon was ruler over all the kingdoms from the River to the Philistines' land and to Egypt's border
p: Traditional, minimalist and middle views disagree about how much of this is history.
b: "The River" is the Euphrates, so the verse describes the borders God promised Abraham (Genesis 15:18). In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 5:1; English Bibles count it as 4:21. The traditional view, held by many evangelical and Jewish scholars (Kenneth Kitchen, Provan, Long and Longman), takes the summary as a fair account of a real kingdom with vassal states, possible in a time when Egypt and Assyria were weak. Minimalist scholars (Thomas Thompson, Niels Peter Lemche) and, more cautiously, Israel Finkelstein read it as later idealization: in the 10th century, they argue, Jerusalem was a modest highland town. A middle view (Amihai Mazar, William Dever) holds that there was a real state under David and Solomon, smaller than these verses suggest, but with building projects and influence beyond the hills. See the united monarchy topic.

a: thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of ordinary flour
p: A cor was a large dry measure, perhaps 60 gallons (220 liters). These amounts would feed thousands.
b: The cor (homer) was the largest dry measure, a donkey-load, estimated at about 220 liters (6 bushels), though some estimates are larger. Ninety cors of flour a day is roughly 20,000 liters. Scholars' estimates of how many people this would feed run from several thousand to well over ten thousand. The figure includes everyone who ate at the king's table: officials, guards, servants and guests (4:27). Lists of the daily provisions of Assyrian palaces show similar royal households.

a: fattened fowl
p: No one knows exactly what the barburim were. Guesses include geese, cuckoos and guinea fowl.
b: Barburim appears only here. Older Jewish commentators guessed fattened fowl or geese; modern guesses include guinea fowl and cuckoos. The animals listed, deer, gazelles and roe deer, were clean game under the law (Deuteronomy 14:5).

a: the whole region Beyond the River
p: "Beyond the River" means west of the Euphrates, as seen from Mesopotamia. Critics take it as a clue to when the verse was written.
b: Ever hannahar means "across the River." Seen from Judah, the land west of the Euphrates was on this side. The phrase is the official name of the Persian province west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:10–11; Nehemiah 2:7), and an Assyrian equivalent is also known. Many critical scholars therefore date this verse to the late monarchy or the exile, written from a Mesopotamian point of view. Traditional readers answer that a standard imperial name could be used by anyone. Tiphsah is probably Thapsacus, a crossing on the middle Euphrates.

a: everyone sitting under his own vine and his own fig tree
t: Under the vine and fig tree
p: The picture of peace and owning your own land, later taken up by the prophets for the coming age.
b: A vine and a fig tree were the signs of a settled farmer who would harvest what he planted. The phrase became the prophets' image of the peace of the last days (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10). 1 Maccabees uses it to praise the peace under Simon, brother of Judas Maccabeus, about 140 BC: "Each one sat under his vine and his fig tree, / and no one was there to frighten them" (1 Maccabees 14:12). Even an Assyrian commander used it to tempt Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:31). George Washington quoted it often in his letters, including to the Jewish congregation at Newport in 1790. "From Dan to Beersheba" is the traditional north-to-south span of Israel (Judges 20:1).
r: Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10; 2 Kings 18:31; Judges 20:1; John 1:48; 1 Maccabees 14:12

a: Solomon kept horses in forty thousand stalls
p: Chronicles gives four thousand stalls. Deuteronomy had warned a king not to gather many horses.
b: 2 Chronicles 9:25 has "four thousand" stalls, and many scholars think forty thousand is a copying error (see the variant). 10:26 gives Solomon 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen. Deuteronomy warns that the king "must not get himself many horses, or send the people back to Egypt to get more horses" (Deuteronomy 17:16), and Solomon traded in horses from Egypt and Kue (10:28–29). The word parashim can mean horsemen or chariot horses.

a: a heart as broad as the sand along the edge of the sea
p: "Breadth of heart" means a wide-ranging mind. Elsewhere a "broad heart" means pride.
b: Rochav lev, "breadth of heart," here means a mind that takes in a great range of knowledge, "as broad as the sand." In Proverbs 21:4 and Psalm 101:5 the same picture, a "wide heart," means arrogance. The narrator uses it as praise; readers who know chapter 11 may hear both senses. "Like the sand" picks up 4:20.

a: the wisdom of all the peoples of the east and all Egypt's wisdom
t: The wisdom of the east and of Egypt
p: Israel's neighbors were famous for wisdom. One Egyptian text is closely parallel to part of Proverbs.
b: "The people of the east" were the tribes of the Syrian and Arabian desert, and Edom; Job came from Uz in the east (Job 1:3), and Edom was known for its wise men (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8). Egypt had a long tradition of written instructions for officials. The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, probably older than Solomon, has thirty chapters and many sayings very close to Proverbs 22:17–24:22, which also speaks of "thirty sayings" (Proverbs 22:20). Most scholars think the Hebrew collection drew on it; a few argue the reverse or a common source.
r: Job 1:3; Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8; Proverbs 22:17–24:22; Genesis 41:8; Acts 7:22

a: Ethan the Ezrahite, than Heman and Calcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol
p: These men were famous for wisdom. Ethan and Heman have psalms named for them.
b: Psalm 88 is titled for "Heman the Ezrahite" and Psalm 89 for "Ethan the Ezrahite." 1 Chronicles 2:6 lists Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara as descendants of Zerah of Judah ("Ezrahite" may mean "of Zerah"), while 1 Chronicles 15:19 names a Heman and an Ethan as Levite singers. "Sons of Mahol" may be a family name, or may mean "sons of the dance," a guild of musicians. The point is that Solomon surpassed the most famous names of his day.

a: Three thousand proverbs came from his lips, and there were one thousand and five of his songs
p: Tradition gives Solomon Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs; the Greek here says five thousand songs.
b: The book of Proverbs has about 900 sayings and names Solomon in its titles (Proverbs 1:1; 10:1; 25:1); Psalms 72 and 127 are titled "of Solomon." The Song of Songs (Song of Songs 1:1) and Ecclesiastes (Ecclesiastes 1:1, "son of David, king in Jerusalem") are traditionally his. A midrash says he wrote the Song in his youth, Proverbs in middle age and Ecclesiastes in old age (Midrash Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1). Most critical scholars date most of these books later and see Solomon as their patron figure. The Greek translation has five thousand songs.
r: Proverbs 1:1; Proverbs 10:1; Proverbs 25:1; Psalm 72:0; Psalm 127:0; Song of Songs 1:1; Ecclesiastes 1:1

a: He talked about trees
p: Later Jewish tradition made Solomon a master of plants, animals, demons and magic.
b: The verse may describe lists of plants and animals like the Egyptian word lists called onomastica, as Albrecht Alt suggested, or proverbs and fables about nature (Proverbs 30:24–31). Later tradition went much further. The Wisdom of Solomon has him claim to know the natures of living creatures, the powers of spirits, and the kinds of plants and the strength of roots (Wisdom 7:20). Josephus says Solomon composed spells for driving out demons, and that he himself saw a Jew named Eleazar use them before the emperor Vespasian (Antiquities 8.45–49). The Testament of Solomon and later legends gave him a ring to command demons. None of this is in Kings. From cedar to hyssop means from the greatest plant to the smallest.

a: They came from all the earth's kings, who had heard about his wisdom
p: The nations coming to hear Solomon prepare for the queen of Sheba (10:1–13).
b: This verse looks ahead to the queen of Sheba, who comes to test Solomon with hard questions (10:1–13). Jesus says the "queen from the south" came "from the far edges of the earth to hear how wise Solomon was. And look, here is something greater than Solomon" (Matthew 12:42). The prophets picture the nations coming to Zion to learn (Isaiah 2:2–3).

a: Hiram, king of Tyre
p: Hiram I of Tyre is also known from Phoenician records quoted by Josephus.
b: In the Hebrew Bible this verse is 5:15; the English count runs 5:1–18 where the Hebrew has 5:15–32. Josephus quotes two writers who used the archives of Tyre, Menander of Ephesus and Dius, who say that Hiram son of Abibaal reigned thirty-four years, built temples in Tyre, and exchanged riddles with Solomon (Against Apion 1.113–120). Josephus also dates the founding of Solomon's temple from Tyre's king list. Tyre was an island city and the leading sea power of the Phoenician coast.

a: Hiram had been a friend of David's for all those years
p: The Hebrew says Hiram was one who "loved" David. In ancient treaties, to "love" meant to be a loyal ally.
b: The phrase is ohev hayah Chiram leDawid, "Hiram was a lover of David." William Moran showed that in ancient Near Eastern treaties and letters, kings who were allies "loved" each other: the word meant loyalty more than feeling. The same sense helps explain Deuteronomy's command to "love the LORD your God" (Deuteronomy 6:5). Hiram had built David's palace (2 Samuel 5:11).

a: because of the war that closed in around him
p: Kings says David was too busy with war. Chronicles says he had shed too much blood.
b: Here Solomon gives a practical reason: David had no rest from enemies. In 2 Samuel 7 God gives another: God had never asked for a house, and David's son would build it (2 Samuel 7:5–13). Chronicles has David say that God told him, "you have shed much blood ... you will not build a house for my name" (1 Chronicles 22:8; 1 Chronicles 28:3). Readers have taken these as different sides of one truth or as different traditions. Ancient Near Eastern kings usually built temples after victories brought peace, as Solomon says.

a: There is no adversary
p: The word is satan, "adversary." Later in Solomon's reign God raises up adversaries against him.
b: Satan here is an ordinary noun, a human opponent, as in 1 Samuel 29:4. The word returns with force in chapter 11, where the LORD "raised up an adversary," a satan, against Solomon: Hadad of Edom and Rezon of Damascus (11:14, 11:23, 11:25). Solomon's boast of peace is true now, and will not stay true.

a: a house for the name of the LORD my God
p: Deuteronomy and Kings speak of a house for God's name. Scholars debate what that phrase means.
b: Deuteronomy speaks of the place where the LORD will "make his name live there" (Deuteronomy 12:11). Gerhard von Rad and many after him thought this "name theology" was a way to say that God himself lives in heaven while only his name dwells in the temple (see 8:27–30). Sandra Richter has argued instead that "to place one's name" is an idiom known from Akkadian royal inscriptions for claiming ownership, as a king set up an inscription with his name. Either way, the temple belongs to the LORD and bears his name. Solomon quotes the promise to David: "He will build a house for my name" (2 Samuel 7:13).

a: Let them cut down cedars in Lebanon for me
p: The cedars of Lebanon were the finest timber of the ancient world, sought by kings of Egypt and Mesopotamia.
b: The tall cedar (Cedrus libani) grew on the Lebanon mountains above the Phoenician coast. Egyptian kings sent for it from the third millennium BC. The Egyptian Story of Wenamun (about 1075 BC) tells of an official sent to Byblos to buy cedar for the god Amun's sacred boat, and of the hard bargaining with the local prince. Mesopotamian kings boasted of cutting cedar for their temples. "Sidonians" was a common name for all Phoenicians (16:31).

a: I will tie it into rafts on the sea
p: Assyrian palace reliefs show Phoenician ships towing logs along the coast.
b: Reliefs from the palace of the Assyrian king Sargon II at Khorsabad (late 8th century BC) show Phoenician boats carrying and towing logs by sea. The place Solomon named was probably Joppa (2 Chronicles 2:16), from which the timber went overland to Jerusalem, about 35 miles (55 kilometers). Ezra's builders brought cedar by the same route (Ezra 3:7).

a: they made a covenant between the two of them
p: Berit, "covenant," here means a treaty between two kings.
b: Berit is the same word used for God's covenant with Israel. Between kings it meant a sworn treaty. Later Hiram calls Solomon "my brother" (9:13), the term for an ally of equal rank. Amos condemns Tyre for forgetting "a covenant of brothers" (Amos 1:9), which some think refers to this treaty.

a: King Solomon drafted a labor force out of all Israel
p: Here Solomon drafts Israelites. 9:22 says he made no Israelite a slave. Readers reconcile this in different ways.
b: This verse says the labor force came "out of all Israel." Later, Kings says Solomon used the remaining Canaanites as slaves but "made no one from the Israelites a slave" (9:22). Many readers distinguish two systems: a rotating draft of Israelites for a few months a year (mas, as here, 5:14) and permanent slave labor for the Canaanites (mas 'oved). Others see two views of Solomon side by side, one critical and one admiring. The northern tribes' complaint that he made their yoke heavy (12:4) supports the first account.

a: three thousand three hundred of them
p: Chronicles gives 3,600 foremen here and 250 over them; Kings 3,300 here and 550 later. Both add up to 3,850.
b: 2 Chronicles 2:18 has 3,600 overseers, and 2 Chronicles 8:10 has 250 chief officers; Kings has 3,300 here and 550 in 9:23. Each pair adds up to 3,850. The Greek of Kings also has 3,600 here (3 Kingdoms 5:30), as reported. Commentators have long noted this: the two books seem to divide the same total differently. Chronicles also says the 150,000 laborers were resident foreigners, not Israelites (2 Chronicles 2:17).

a: great stones, stones of high value
p: Finely cut blocks were a mark of royal building in Israel, seen at Megiddo, Samaria and elsewhere.
b: Smooth-faced cut blocks, called ashlar, laid in courses with headers and stretchers, are found in royal buildings in Israel from the 10th or 9th century BC onward, for example at Megiddo and Samaria. The style is often called Phoenician. The great foundation stones visible today around the Temple Mount are from Herod's rebuilding, about 1,000 years later, not from Solomon's day.

a: the men of Gebal
p: Gebal was the Phoenician city the Greeks called Byblos, famous for its craftsmen.
b: Gebal (modern Jbeil, north of Beirut) was one of the oldest cities on the coast. The Greeks called it Byblos, and because papyrus came through it, its name became the Greek word for a book, which gives us "Bible." Ezekiel mentions the skilled men of Gebal who repaired Tyre's ships (Ezekiel 27:9).

a: Four hundred and eighty years had passed since the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt
p: This verse is the Bible's main anchor for dating the exodus. Readers take the number as exact or as twelve generations.
b: Solomon's fourth year is usually dated about 967/966 BC. Counting 480 years back gives about 1446 BC for the exodus, the date held by many conservative scholars (Bryant Wood, Eugene Merrill). Many others, including some evangelicals (Kenneth Kitchen, James Hoffmeier), date the exodus about 1260 BC, because Exodus 1:11 names the city Rameses and the archaeology of Canaan fits the 13th century better. They read 480 as twelve generations of forty years, a symbolic count. The Greek translation has 440 years. See the date-of-exodus topic. Ziv ("brightness"), the second month, is April–May.

a: in the month of Ziv
p: Ziv, Ethanim and Bul are old Canaanite month names. Later Jews used Babylonian names.
b: Kings uses three old month names: Ziv (the 2nd month, 6:1), Ethanim (the 7th, 8:2) and Bul (the 8th, 6:38). Bul and Ethanim are also found in Phoenician inscriptions. After the exile the Jews used the Babylonian names still used today (Nisan, Iyyar, Tishri, Marcheshvan), and the narrator explains the old names by number, as if readers might no longer know them.

a: sixty cubits in length, twenty in width and thirty cubits in height
p: About 90 by 30 by 45 feet (27 by 9 by 13.5 meters): not huge, but twice the tabernacle.
b: A cubit, the length from elbow to fingertip, was about 18 inches (45 centimeters); a "royal" cubit was a handbreadth longer, about 20.5 inches (52 centimeters). Chronicles says the measures were "by the old standard" (2 Chronicles 3:3). On the common cubit the house was about 90 feet long, 30 feet wide and 45 feet high (27 by 9 by 13.5 meters), not counting the porch and side rooms. The tabernacle was 30 by 10 cubits; the temple doubles it. It was a royal chapel, small beside the great temples of Egypt; most worshipers stood in the courtyards.

a: The porch in front of the great hall of the house
p: The temple had a porch, a great hall and an inner room in a line. Temples of the same plan have been found in Syria and Turkey.
b: The house had three parts in a line: the porch (ulam), the great hall (hekhal, "palace"), and the inner room (devir). Temples with this plan, from about 1300–800 BC, have been excavated at 'Ain Dara in northern Syria and at Tell Tayinat in southern Turkey; 'Ain Dara even had a corridor running around three sides of the shrine, something like the temple's side rooms, and carved lions and cherub-like figures. John Monson has called it the closest known parallel to Solomon's temple. A smaller Israelite temple of the 10th–9th century BC has also been found at Motza, just west of Jerusalem.

a: windows, framed and fixed shut
p: The Hebrew is unclear. Suggestions include latticed, recessed, narrow or high windows.
b: Challonei shequfim atumim is literally "windows of frames, closed." The second word may mean beams or frames, or "looking through"; the third may mean barred, latticed, narrowing inward, or non-opening. Ezekiel's temple has similar windows (Ezekiel 40:16; 41:16). Since the side rooms rose to about fifteen cubits (6:10), any windows in the great hall must have been high in the walls.

a: side rooms all around
p: Three stories of side rooms surrounded the house, probably for storing temple treasures and supplies.
b: The side rooms (tsela'ot, "ribs") ran around the walls of the great hall and the inner room in three stories. They probably held the gifts and treasures that later kings dedicated or took away (7:51; 14:26; 15:18). Ezekiel's temple has thirty side rooms on each of three levels (Ezekiel 41:5–7). The beams of the stories rested on ledges in the outer wall, which grew thinner as it rose (6:6).

a: no sound of hammer or ax or any iron tool was heard in the house
p: Stones were finished at the quarry. Jewish tradition told of a stone-cutting worm, the shamir.
b: The law forbade cutting an altar's stones: "If you have swung your blade over it, you have made it unholy" (Exodus 20:25; Deuteronomy 27:5–6). Kings applies a similar respect to the whole house. The rabbis told of the shamir, a tiny creature created at twilight on the sixth day (Mishnah Avot 5:6) that could split stone, and of how Solomon got it from Ashmedai, king of demons (Bavli Gittin 68a–b). Readers have also taken the silence as a picture of God's work, done quietly and well (1 Peter 2:5).

a: if you live by my rules, and do what my rulings say
t: A word in the middle of the building
p: God's word breaks into the building report. The Greek leaves it out.
b: In the middle of the measurements comes a short word from the LORD, with a condition: the house will not secure God's presence by itself; obedience will. Jeremiah later attacks the idea that the temple protects Jerusalem whatever its people do (Jeremiah 7:4–15). The Old Greek translation lacks 6:11–14 (see the variant), and many scholars think the passage was added to the Hebrew by a later editor. Others think the Greek translator skipped a passage that interrupted the description.

a: I will dwell in the middle of the Israelites
p: The verb shakhan, "dwell," gives the word mishkan, "tabernacle."
b: Shakhanti betokh benei Yisra'el echoes the purpose of the tabernacle: "They are to make me a holy place, and I will live in their midst" (Exodus 25:8; compare Exodus 29:45). Later Jewish writers used the related word Shekhinah for God's dwelling presence. John says the Word "pitched his tent" among us (John 1:14), using a Greek verb that sounds like the Hebrew.

a: the beams of the ceiling
p: The Hebrew says "the walls of the ceiling"; the Plain reads "beams" with the Greek, here and in 6:16.
b: In 6:15 and 6:16 the Hebrew has qirot, "walls," which makes little sense for the top of the room. The Greek reads "beams," which in Hebrew (qorot) differs only in a vowel letter, and most translators follow it, as the Plain does. In 6:17 the Hebrew lifnay, "before me," is obscure; the Plain takes it as "in front of" the inner room, as most commentators do.

a: the inner room, the most holy place
p: The devir was the innermost room. Older English Bibles call it the "oracle."
b: Devir probably means "back room" (from a root meaning "behind"). Jerome's Latin connected it with davar, "word," and rendered it oraculum, so the King James Version says "oracle." It is also called "the most holy place" (qodesh haqqodashim), the name used for the tabernacle's inner room (Exodus 26:33). Only the high priest entered it, once a year (Leviticus 16; Hebrews 9:7).

a: twenty cubits in length, twenty in width and twenty in height
p: The inner room was a cube, 30 feet (9 meters) each way. The new Jerusalem in Revelation is also a cube.
b: The inner room was twenty cubits each way, about 30 feet (9 meters), and covered with gold. The house was thirty cubits high (6:2), so the inner room had either a raised floor or a lower ceiling than the hall; scholars debate which. A cube is the most complete of shapes. The new Jerusalem in Revelation is a cube: "Its length, width, and height were equal" (Revelation 21:16), as if the whole city has become the most holy place, and it has no temple (Revelation 21:22).

a: refined gold
p: Zahav sagur, literally "closed gold," probably means refined or solid gold.
b: Zahav sagur is found only in Kings and Chronicles. It may mean gold that has been refined ("shut up" in a crucible) or gold kept in the royal treasury. Ancient temples were often covered in gold leaf or plate; Mesopotamian and Egyptian kings boast of it in their building texts. Shishak of Egypt later carried off the gold (14:25–26).

a: two cherubim from the wood of olive trees
p: Two winged guardian figures, 15 feet (4.5 meters) tall, filled the inner room from wall to wall.
b: A cherub (plural cherubim) was a winged guardian, part human, part animal, like the winged lions and bulls that guarded Assyrian palaces. On the ark two small gold cherubim faced each other over the lid (Exodus 25:18–20). Solomon's pair stood ten cubits high, facing the hall (2 Chronicles 3:13), their wings touching the walls and each other (6:27). Together they formed the throne of the LORD, "who sits on the cherubim as his throne" (1 Samuel 4:4), with the ark as his footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2). Atse shemen, "oil-wood," may be olive or a resinous wood such as pine.
r: Exodus 25:18–22; 1 Samuel 4:4; 2 Chronicles 3:10–13; 1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 99:1; Ezekiel 10

a: cherubim, palm trees and opening blossoms
p: The carved cherubim, palms and flowers make the temple a picture of Eden.
b: Cherubim guarded the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24), and the temple's walls and doors are carved with cherubim among palm trees and flowers, overlaid with gold, the metal of the land of Eden (Genesis 2:11–12). Many scholars, Jewish and Christian (Jon Levenson, Gregory Beale), see the temple as a picture of the garden where God walked with humans, and Ezekiel's temple has a river flowing out to give life (Ezekiel 47:1–12). The psalmist pictures the righteous "planted in the LORD's house" like palm trees (Psalm 92:12–13).
r: Genesis 2:8–14; Genesis 3:24; Ezekiel 41:18–20; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Psalm 92:12–13; Revelation 22:1–2

a: Its doorframe and posts had five sides
p: The Hebrew says only "fifth." It may mean five-sided, five steps of molding, or one fifth of the wall.
b: The phrase ha'ayil mezuzot chamishit is very obscure. Some take it as a five-sided frame, a lintel shaped like a gable; some as a frame with five recessed steps, as in some ancient temples; others as a doorway one fifth of the wall's width. 6:33 uses "fourth" for the doors of the great hall in the same way.

a: three layers of cut stone and a layer of cedar beams
p: Laying a course of timber between courses of stone was a known building method in Syria and Anatolia.
b: Courses of wooden beams set between layers of stone helped walls absorb earthquakes. The method is known from Late Bronze and Iron Age buildings in Syria and Anatolia. The decree of Cyrus for rebuilding the temple uses the same pattern: "three courses of large stones and one course of new timber" (Ezra 6:4).

a: Seven years he had worked to build it
p: The temple took seven years; Solomon's own house took thirteen (7:1). Is that praise or criticism?
b: From the month of Ziv in the fourth year to Bul in the eleventh is seven and a half years, rounded to seven, a fitting number for a holy house.
