The next verse says Solomon spent thirteen years on his own house (7:1). Some readers, ancient and modern, see a quiet rebuke: he took twice as long for himself. Others answer that the palace complex was much larger (7:2–12), and that Josephus and many rabbis took the seven years as zeal, because Solomon hurried God's house. The house was finished in the eighth month but dedicated in the seventh (8:2), either eleven months later or after the palace was done as well (9:1).

a: His own house Solomon was thirteen years in building
p: Solomon's palace complex stood south of the temple. The Greek tells it after the temple's furnishings.
b: The palace buildings of 7:1–12, the House of the Forest of Lebanon, the Porch of Pillars, the throne room, Solomon's own house and the house for Pharaoh's daughter, lay between the temple and the old City of David. Nothing certain of them has been found. In the Greek translation this whole section comes after 7:51, so that the temple and its furnishings are described without a break; see the variant. The arrangement in either text shows the temple as part of a royal complex, as temples in Syria and Mesopotamia often were.

a: the House of the Forest of Lebanon
p: The great hall got its name from its rows of cedar pillars. It held Solomon's gold shields.
b: The building was 100 by 50 cubits and 30 high, about 150 by 75 by 45 feet (45 by 22.5 by 13.5 meters), larger than the temple itself. Its rows of cedar pillars looked like a forest. Solomon kept his 500 gold shields there (10:17), and Isaiah calls it "the House of the Forest" where the weapons were stored (Isaiah 22:8). The Hebrew says four rows of pillars, and the Greek three. Some commentators read the forty-five "in rows of fifteen" of 7:3 as pillars, which would suggest three rows; others take them as side rooms or beams, which leaves four rows possible.

a: the throne porch, where he would give judgments, the Porch of Judgment
p: The king heard cases from his throne in a public hall.
b: In Israel the king was the highest court of appeal (3:16–28; 2 Samuel 15:2–4). His ivory and gold throne (10:18–20) probably stood in this hall. "From one floor to the other" may mean the whole floor was paneled, or the text may once have read "from the floor to the rafters" (with a small change of letters, as in 6:15–16).

a: for Pharaoh's daughter, whom Solomon had taken as wife, he made a house
p: Chronicles says Solomon moved her out of the City of David because the ark had made it holy.
b: Pharaoh's daughter had lived in the City of David until this house was built (3:1; 9:24). Chronicles explains: Solomon said, "No wife of mine will live in the house of David king of Israel, because the places the LORD's ark has come into are holy" (2 Chronicles 8:11). Kings gives no reason.

a: His mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali
p: This Hiram is a bronze worker, not the king. Chronicles says his mother was from Dan.
b: This Hiram (called Huram-abi in 2 Chronicles 2:13) is a craftsman of mixed birth: an Israelite mother and a Tyrian father. Chronicles says "his mother came from the daughters of Dan" (2 Chronicles 2:14). Jewish commentators reconciled the two: Rashi says his mother was from Dan and his father from Naphtali; Radak suggests a Danite woman widowed from a husband of Naphtali. The Chronicler's "Dan" may also be meant to recall Oholiab of Dan, Bezalel's partner in making the tabernacle (Exodus 31:6).

a: Hiram was filled with skill, understanding and know-how
p: The words for Hiram's gifts are the words used for Bezalel, the maker of the tabernacle.
b: God says of Bezalel, "I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill, with understanding, with know-how, and with every kind of craft" (Exodus 31:3). Chokhmah, "skill" or "wisdom," is the same word used for Solomon's wisdom (3:28; 4:29). In the Bible wisdom includes a craftsman's skill. The temple, like the tabernacle, is built by gifted workers, though Kings does not say, as Exodus does of Bezalel, that Hiram was filled with "the Spirit of God."

a: The first pillar stood eighteen cubits high
p: Each pillar was about 27 feet (8 meters) high and nearly 6 feet (1.8 meters) thick, hollow cast bronze.
b: The Hebrew gives the height of one pillar and the girth of the other, meaning both. Eighteen cubits is about 27 feet (8 meters); a girth of twelve cubits, about 18 feet (5.4 meters), gives a diameter of nearly 6 feet. Jeremiah adds that they were hollow, four fingers thick (Jeremiah 52:21), and the Greek of Kings has the same detail here, as reported. Chronicles has 35 cubits, perhaps for both together (2 Chronicles 3:15). The Babylonians broke them up for scrap (2 Kings 25:13). Free-standing pillars flanked the doors of temples at 'Ain Dara and Tell Tayinat, and Herodotus describes two pillars at the temple of Melqart in Tyre, "one of refined gold, the other of emerald" (Histories 2.44).

a: called its name Jakin
p: The names may mean "He establishes" and "In him is strength."
b: Yakhin probably means "he will establish" and Bo'az "in him is strength." R. B. Y. Scott suggested that they were the first words of inscriptions or royal prayers on the pillars, such as "He (the LORD) will establish the throne of David" and "In the strength of the LORD the king rejoices" (compare 2 Samuel 7:12–13; Psalm 21:1). Others think they were names of a priestly family or simply symbols of stability. Boaz is also the name of David's ancestor (Ruth 4:21), but no ancient source links the two. The names later became symbols in Freemasonry.

a: He made the Sea out of cast metal
p: The great bronze basin held water for the priests' washing and stood for the sea that God rules.
b: Chronicles says, "The Sea, though, was where the priests washed" (2 Chronicles 4:6). But its name and size suggest more. In Canaanite myth, the god Baal defeats Yam, "Sea"; in the Bible the LORD rules the sea and sets its bounds (Psalm 93:3–4; Job 38:8–11). Many scholars, such as Carol Meyers and Jon Levenson, read the Sea as a sign that the chaos waters are tamed in God's house. Babylon's temples had a basin called apsu, "the deep." The Sea in heaven, "like glass," stands before God's throne in Revelation (Revelation 4:6; Revelation 15:2). King Ahaz later took it off the oxen (2 Kings 16:17).
r: 2 Chronicles 4:2–6; Psalm 93:3–4; Job 38:8–11; Revelation 4:6; Revelation 15:2; 2 Kings 16:17; 2 Kings 25:13

a: From one lip to the other it was ten cubits
t: Does the Bible say pi is 3?
p: Ten across and thirty around gives pi = 3. There are several reasonable explanations.
b: A circle ten cubits across has a circumference of about 31.4 cubits. Explanations: the numbers are rounded, as builders often did; the width was measured across the outer lip, which flared like a lily (7:26), while the cord went around the narrower body; or the thickness of a handbreadth makes the difference between inside and outside measures. An idea often credited to the 18th-century Vilna Gaon notes that the word for "line" is written qweh (Ketiv) but read qaw (Qere), and that the ratio of their letter values, 111 to 106, times 3 gives 3.1415. That is a clever coincidence, not something the writer intended. The verse is not trying to state a mathematical constant.

a: gourd shapes
p: Chronicles has "oxen" under the Sea's rim, a one-letter difference in Hebrew.
b: Kings has peqa'im, "gourds," the same ornament as the carved gourds of 6:18. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 4:3 has beqarim, "oxen," perhaps influenced by the twelve oxen under the Sea (7:25). The Hebrew words differ by one letter. Most scholars think "gourds" is original.

a: It stood on twelve oxen
p: The twelve bronze oxen probably stood for the twelve tribes, or for strength and fertility.
b: The oxen faced the four directions in threes. Many readers connect them with the twelve tribes camped around the tabernacle in four groups of three (Numbers 2). The bull was also a common symbol of strength and of gods in Canaan; the same bull image will be Jeroboam's golden calves (12:28). Here they serve the LORD's house. Ahaz removed them, probably to pay tribute to Assyria (2 Kings 16:17).

a: It could hold two thousand baths
p: A bath was about 6 gallons (22 liters), so the Sea held about 11,600 gallons (44,000 liters).
b: The bath was a liquid measure of about 22 liters (5.8 gallons), estimates range from 21 to 23 liters. Two thousand baths is about 44,000 liters (11,600 gallons). Chronicles has three thousand (2 Chronicles 4:5; see the variant); some scholars think Chronicles gives its full capacity and Kings its usual filling, others that one figure is a copying error. A "handbreadth" is about 3 inches (7.5 centimeters).

a: Next he made the stands, ten of them, out of bronze
p: Small bronze stands on wheels with figures of lions and cherubs have been found in Cyprus.
b: Each stand was four cubits square and three high, about 6 by 6 by 4.5 feet (1.8 by 1.8 by 1.35 meters), and carried a basin holding forty baths (7:38), nearly 900 liters. Filled, each would weigh well over a ton. Miniature bronze stands on four wheels, with panels showing animals and winged figures, have been found in Cyprus from about 1200–1100 BC, and they help explain these hard verses (7:28–37), whose technical terms are not fully understood.

a: between Succoth and Zarethan
t: Bronze foundries in the Jordan valley
p: The bronze was cast in clay soil in the Jordan valley, near Succoth.
b: Succoth is usually placed at Tell Deir Alla, east of the Jordan near the Jabbok river, where excavators found evidence of metalworking furnaces. The valley's clay made good molds, and the work, with its heat and smoke, was best done far from the city. Zarethan's location is uncertain (Joshua 3:16).

a: the table of gold where the Presence Bread was laid
p: The tabernacle had one table and one lampstand; Solomon's temple had ten lampstands.
b: The tabernacle had one table for the Presence Bread and one seven-branched lampstand (Exodus 25:23–40). Solomon placed ten lampstands before the inner room, five on each side (7:49), and Chronicles says ten tables (2 Chronicles 4:8). The single seven-branched menorah returned in the second temple; the Arch of Titus in Rome shows the one the Romans carried off in AD 70.

a: the holy gifts of David his father
p: David had set apart the spoils of his wars for the LORD.
b: David set apart the silver and gold of the nations he conquered (2 Samuel 8:11–12). Chronicles adds that he gathered huge stores of materials for the temple (1 Chronicles 22:14; 1 Chronicles 29:2–5). Solomon puts them in the temple treasury, which later kings would raid to pay off enemies (14:26; 15:18; 2 Kings 18:15).

a: to bring the ark of the LORD's covenant up out of the City of David, that is, Zion
p: The ark was carried a short distance north and uphill, from the old city to the temple.
b: The City of David stood on the narrow ridge south of the temple mount (2 Samuel 5:7). The ark had been in David's tent there (2 Samuel 6:17). The procession went only a few hundred yards north and uphill. Later, "Zion" came to mean the temple mount and all Jerusalem (Psalm 2:6; Isaiah 2:3).

a: in the month of Ethanim, at the feast. That is the seventh month
p: "The feast" in the seventh month is the Feast of Booths (Sukkot), Israel's great autumn festival.
b: Ethanim ("ever-flowing") is the later Tishri, September–October. The feast of that month is Sukkot, the Feast of Booths, the harvest festival called simply "the feast" (8:65; 12:32; Leviticus 23:33–36). Deuteronomy commands that the law be read to all Israel at that feast (Deuteronomy 31:10–11). Jeroboam will set up a rival feast in the eighth month (12:32–33).

a: with the tent of meeting and all the holy objects that were in the tent
p: The old tent of meeting was brought into the temple, probably to be stored.
b: The tent of meeting had stood at Gibeon (2 Chronicles 1:3). Bringing it up joins the old worship of the wilderness to the new house. It was probably stored in the side rooms. Some scholars think "the tent of meeting" here means David's tent in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6:17). Rabbinic tradition said the tabernacle was stored beneath the temple (Bavli Sotah 9a).

a: They have stayed there until today
p: The writer speaks as if the ark were still in place. Either the source is older than 586 BC, or the phrase was copied.
b: The temple and, presumably, the ark were destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:9). The phrase "until today" suggests a source written while the temple stood. Many scholars think the Deuteronomistic History was first written under King Josiah (about 620 BC) and updated in the exile, and that phrases like this survive from the earlier edition (Frank Moore Cross). Others think the exilic editor simply copied his source. Chronicles copies the phrase (2 Chronicles 5:9) long after it could have been literally true.

a: The poles were long
p: The Bible never says what became of the ark. Jewish tradition has several answers.
b: The ark is last mentioned in Josiah's day (2 Chronicles 35:3). Jeremiah says that one day people will no longer speak of it or miss it (Jeremiah 3:16). The Babylonian Talmud records the view that Josiah hid it beneath the temple (Bavli Yoma 52b), and 2 Maccabees says Jeremiah hid it in a cave on Mount Nebo (2 Maccabees 2:4–8). The Ethiopian Orthodox Church holds that it was taken to Ethiopia by Menelik, son of Solomon and the queen of Sheba, a tradition recorded in the Kebra Nagast. Most historians think it was destroyed or carried off by Babylon.

a: Nothing was inside the ark but the two tablets of stone
p: Hebrews mentions the jar of manna and Aaron's staff too. The Old Testament places them in front of the ark.
b: Hebrews 9:4 lists "the golden jar holding the manna, Aaron's staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant" in the ark. In Exodus and Numbers the manna and the staff were put "before the testimony," that is, in front of the ark (Exodus 16:33–34; Numbers 17:10). Kings insists that by Solomon's day only the tablets were inside. Readers explain the difference as a shift in how "in" and "before" were used, or as items lost before the temple period. Horeb is Deuteronomy's name for Mount Sinai.

a: The LORD's glory filled the LORD's house
p: As at the tabernacle, the cloud of glory fills the new house, and the priests cannot stay.
b: The scene repeats the end of Exodus: "The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34), and Moses could not go in (Exodus 40:35). Chronicles adds fire from heaven on the offerings (2 Chronicles 7:1). Ezekiel later sees the glory leave the temple before its fall (Ezekiel 10:18–19) and return to a new temple (Ezekiel 43:1–5). John says of Jesus, "we saw his glory" (John 1:14).
r: Exodus 40:34–35; 2 Chronicles 5:13–14; 2 Chronicles 7:1–3; Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 43:1–5; John 1:14

a: he will live in the thick dark cloud
p: Arafel is the dense storm cloud in which God came to Sinai.
b: Arafel is the dark cloud on Mount Sinai: Moses "went up close to the deep darkness where God was" (Exodus 20:21; Deuteronomy 4:11). The psalms use it for God's hidden majesty (Psalm 18:11; Psalm 97:2). Solomon's short poem pairs God's choice of darkness with Solomon's building of a fixed house: God who cannot be seen now has a place on earth.

a: I have built you a princely house
p: Zevul means "lofty" or "princely." The same word is in the name of the god Baal-zebul.
b: Beit zevul is "a house of exaltation" or "a princely dwelling." In the Ugaritic poems from Syria (about 1300 BC), zbl, "prince," is a title of Baal, "Prince Baal." The Philistine god Baal-zebub of 2 Kings 1:2 is probably a mocking change of Baal-zebul, "Baal the prince," to "lord of flies," and the Gospels' Beelzebul keeps the older form (Matthew 12:24). Here the title goes to the LORD's house.

a: But I chose David to be over my people Israel
p: Chronicles' version adds that God chose Jerusalem as well as David. A Qumran fragment may agree.
b: Here God says only that he chose no city, but chose David. In Chronicles the verse runs: "I have chosen no city out of all Israel's tribes as the place to build a house where my name would be. Nor did I choose any man to be ruler over my people Israel. But I chose Jerusalem for my name to be there, and I chose David to be over my people Israel" (2 Chronicles 6:5–6). The extra words may have dropped out of Kings by a copyist's eye skipping (see the variant). Psalm 78:67–72 and Psalm 132:13 join the two choices, of Zion and of David.

a: He lifted his open palms to the heavens
p: Solomon stood with hands raised, then knelt (8:54). Chronicles places him on a bronze platform.
b: Standing with arms raised and palms open was a common posture of prayer (Exodus 9:29; Psalm 28:2; 1 Timothy 2:8). At the end Solomon is on his knees (8:54), as Ezra later knelt (Ezra 9:5) and Daniel prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:10). Chronicles explains that Solomon stood and knelt on a bronze platform five cubits square in the courtyard (2 Chronicles 6:13). Jews traditionally stand for the central prayer, the Amidah, whose name means "standing."
r: 8:54; Exodus 9:29; Psalm 28:2; Ezra 9:5; Daniel 6:10; 2 Chronicles 6:12–13; 1 Timothy 2:8

a: not in the heavens above, and not on the earth below, is there any God like you
p: Solomon's prayer begins with the confession that the LORD is beyond compare.
b: The words recall the Song at the Sea, "Who is like you among the gods, O LORD?" (Exodus 15:11), and Moses' words that the LORD is God "in the sky above and on the earth below" (Deuteronomy 4:39). "Keep covenant and loyal love" is Deuteronomy's phrase (Deuteronomy 7:9). Daniel and Nehemiah begin their prayers in the same way (Daniel 9:4; Nehemiah 1:5).

a: But can God truly make his home on earth?
p: At the height of the dedication, Solomon says no building can contain God.
b: This is the theological center of the prayer. The temple is not God's home in the way pagan temples housed their gods' statues; God lives "in the heavens" (8:30, 8:39, 8:43) and hears from there, while his name is in the house (8:29). Jewish readers took this as the basis of prayer toward the temple, and later of prayer anywhere: Jon Levenson calls the chapter a bridge "from temple to synagogue." Christian readers hear it in Stephen's speech, "the Most High does not live in houses made by hands" (Acts 7:48–50), and in John's claim that Jesus' body is the temple (John 2:19–21). Critical scholars often see here the Deuteronomistic "name theology" of the exile, when there was no temple. Isaiah 66:1 makes the same point.

a: Listen to the prayer your servant prays toward this place
p: Jews pray facing Jerusalem, a practice rooted in this prayer.
b: Solomon asks God to hear prayers prayed "toward this place," even from far away (8:35, 8:38, 8:44, 8:48). Daniel prayed in Babylon with his windows open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10). The Talmud rules that a Jew outside the land should face the land of Israel, in the land face Jerusalem, in Jerusalem face the temple, and in the temple face the most holy place (Bavli Berakhot 30a). Synagogues are still built to face Jerusalem. Early Muslims also first prayed toward Jerusalem before turning toward Mecca.

a: Hear, and forgive
p: The refrain "hear ... and forgive" runs through the whole prayer.
b: Wesham'ta wesalachta, "hear and forgive," is the prayer's refrain (8:30, 8:34, 8:36, 8:39, 8:50). The verb salach, "forgive," is used in the Bible only with God as its subject: only God forgives in this sense. Seven cases follow (8:31–51), a full list of what could go wrong in Israel's life.

a: a curse oath is laid on him to make him swear
p: When there were no witnesses, a person could be made to swear an oath of innocence before God.
b: Some cases could not be proved, such as goods left in a neighbor's care that went missing (Exodus 22:7–11). The accused swore an alah, an oath with a curse on himself if he lied, and the case was left to God (compare Numbers 5:19–22). Solomon asks God to act as judge, condemning the guilty and clearing the innocent, the same task God gave Solomon in chapter 3.

a: acknowledge your name
p: The verb hodah means to acknowledge, confess, give thanks or praise.
b: Wehodu et-shemekha can mean "praise your name" or "confess your name," that is, admit that you are just in what you did. The King James Version has "confess." The same verb gives todah, a thank offering, and hodu, "give thanks" (Psalm 136:1). Here, after defeat, the sense is to admit God's justice and turn back.

a: Say the sky is locked shut and no rain falls
p: Deuteronomy warns that God will shut the sky if Israel serves other gods. In Elijah's day he does.
b: Deuteronomy warns: "He will shut up the sky, and there will be no rain" (Deuteronomy 11:17), and Leviticus and Deuteronomy list drought among the covenant curses (Leviticus 26:19; Deuteronomy 28:23–24). Elijah's drought under Ahab will be the great example in Kings (17:1; 18:41–45). James uses Elijah's prayer for rain as a model (James 5:17–18). "Pressing them down" translates ta'anem, "you humble them"; some read "you answer them."

a: Say there is hunger in the land, or deadly disease, or crops scorched or moldy
p: The list of disasters follows Deuteronomy 28's list of curses.
b: Famine, plague, blight, mildew, locusts and siege are the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 (Deuteronomy 28:21–22, 28:38, 28:52). Amos says God sent them and still Israel did not return (Amos 4:6–11). Solomon's prayer turns the list of curses into a list of reasons to pray. On "the land where their towns are," literally "the land of their gates," see Deuteronomy 28:52.
r: Deuteronomy 28:21–22; Deuteronomy 28:38–42; Deuteronomy 28:52; Leviticus 26:16–26; Amos 4:6–11; Joel 1:4

a: the wound in his own heart
p: Nega' levavo is "the plague of his heart": each person's own pain, or his own guilt.
b: Nega' is a blow or plague, the word used for the outbreaks of disease in 8:37. Here it moves inside: each person knows his own heart's sickness. The phrase may mean grief or guilt. Jeremiah calls the heart "deceitful above all things and beyond cure" (Jeremiah 17:9). The King James Version's "the plague of his own heart" became a well-known phrase among the Puritans.

a: And the foreigner too, the one who is not from your people Israel
t: A house of prayer for all peoples
p: Solomon asks God to hear the prayers of foreigners. The prophets and Jesus take up the hope.
b: A nokhri is someone from another nation, not a resident foreigner (ger). Solomon expects foreigners to hear of the LORD and come to pray, and he asks God to answer them so that "all the earth's peoples will know your name" (8:43). Isaiah says, "my house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples" (Isaiah 56:7), and Jesus quotes it when he clears the temple courts (Mark 11:17). Naaman (2 Kings 5) and the queen of Sheba (10:1–13) are foreigners who come to know the LORD.

a: your name has been called over this house
p: To have a name called over something meant to own it.
b: In Hebrew, to "call one's name over" something is to claim it, as a conqueror might name a city (2 Samuel 12:28) or a man take a wife (Isaiah 4:1). The temple belongs to the LORD; so does Israel, "called by my name" (2 Chronicles 7:14). See the note on 5:5.

a: since there is no human being who never sins
t: No one who does not sin
p: Solomon's aside about universal sin is echoed in Ecclesiastes and Paul.
b: Ecclesiastes says almost the same: "there is no human being on the earth so righteous that he does good and does not sin" (Ecclesiastes 7:20). Paul draws on such texts for his teaching that all have sinned (Romans 3:23). Christian theology often reads this as part of the doctrine of original sin. Jewish teaching agrees that no one is without sin, and speaks of the inclination to evil (yetzer hara) that every person must master, with repentance always open (8:47). Both read the prayer as hope for sinners.

a: Say their captors carry them off as prisoners to the enemy's land
p: The last case is exile. Readers debate whether this was written before or after the exile happened.
b: Traditional readers point out that the threat of exile is part of the covenant curses in the Law (Leviticus 26:33, 26:40–45; Deuteronomy 28:36, 28:64; Deuteronomy 30:1–5), and that kings of the time knew whole peoples could be deported. Most critical scholars think the prayer, at least 8:44–53, was shaped in the exile after 586 BC, when the temple was gone and prayer "toward the land" was all that was left. Some, like Jon Levenson, see two layers: an older dedication and an exilic expansion. Both readings agree that the prayer gave exiles words to return to God.
r: Leviticus 26:33; Leviticus 26:40–45; Deuteronomy 28:36; Deuteronomy 28:64; Deuteronomy 30:1–5; 2 Kings 25:21

a: 'We have sinned. We have gone wrong. We have done evil,'
p: This three-part confession became a fixed form, used by Daniel, in the psalms, and on the Day of Atonement.
b: The three verbs, chata'nu, he'ewinu, rasha'nu, appear again in Psalm 106:6 and Daniel 9:5. The Mishnah gives the high priest's confession on the Day of Atonement in a similar three-part form: "I have done wrong, I have rebelled, I have sinned" (Mishnah Yoma 3:8; 4:2). The Jewish prayer book's confessions for Yom Kippur grew from these. "Take it to heart" is literally "bring it back to their heart," a play on shuv, "turn back" (8:47–48).

a: Let their captors look on them with pity
p: Solomon asks God to move the hearts of Israel's conquerors. The psalms and Ezra see it happen.
b: Psalm 106 says God caused Israel to be pitied by all who held them captive (Psalm 106:46). Ezra and Nehemiah tell how Persian kings let the exiles go home and rebuild (Ezra 1:1–4; Nehemiah 2:1–8). Kings itself ends with a small sign of it: Jehoiachin released from prison and given a seat at the Babylonian king's table (2 Kings 25:27–30).

a: out from the middle of the iron furnace
p: Egypt was "the iron furnace," a smelter that refined Israel.
b: Moses called Egypt "the iron furnace" (Deuteronomy 4:20), and Jeremiah uses the phrase too (Jeremiah 11:4). A furnace for iron was the hottest fire people knew. The phrase pictures slavery as a smelter from which God drew his people out. Solomon reminds God that the people in exile are still the ones he rescued.

a: He has given his people Israel a resting place
p: Solomon declares God's promise of rest fulfilled, in Joshua's words.
b: Deuteronomy had said Israel had "not come to the resting place" (Deuteronomy 12:9) and that God would give them rest (Deuteronomy 12:10). Joshua said, "Not one of all the good words the LORD had spoken to the house of Israel fell short" (Joshua 21:45). Now, with the ark at rest (8:6; Psalm 132:8, 132:14), Solomon says the same. Hebrews later argues that the true rest is still to come (Hebrews 4:8–11).
r: Deuteronomy 12:9–10; Joshua 21:45; Joshua 23:14; 2 Samuel 7:1; Psalm 132:8; Psalm 132:14; Hebrews 4:8–11

a: the LORD is God. There is no other
p: Solomon ends with the confession of Deuteronomy 4, and the hope that every nation will make it.
b: Moses had said, "the LORD is God in the sky above and on the earth below. There is no other" (Deuteronomy 4:39). Elijah's contest on Carmel will end with the people crying, "The LORD, he is the God!" (18:39). Solomon's prayer looks beyond Israel to "every people on earth" (compare 8:43; Isaiah 45:22).

a: let your heart be whole with the LORD our God
p: Lev shalem, a "whole heart," plays on Solomon's name. In 11:4 his heart is not whole.
b: Shalem, "whole, complete, at peace," is from the same root as shalom and Solomon's name, Shelomoh. Solomon asks the people for a heart "whole" with the LORD. The reader of Kings will hear the echo in 11:4: "His heart was not whole with the LORD his God the way his father David's heart had been" (11:4).

a: twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep
p: The numbers are enormous. Readers take them as exact, rounded, or royal exaggeration.
b: Chronicles gives the same figures (2 Chronicles 7:5). Over fourteen days (8:65) that is about 1,600 cattle and 8,500 sheep a day. Some readers take the numbers as they stand: the whole nation was present and most of the meat of peace offerings was eaten by the worshipers. Others suggest the figures are inflated in copying or in royal style; Assyrian kings recorded similar huge banquets, such as Ashurnasirpal II's feast for 69,574 guests at Kalhu. The text itself admits that the altar could not hold them all (8:64).

a: dedicated the LORD's house
p: The verb chanakh, "dedicate," gives the word Hanukkah.
b: Chanakh means to dedicate, to begin the use of something (Deuteronomy 20:5). Its noun, chanukkah, "dedication," is used for the altar (Numbers 7:10) and for this temple (2 Chronicles 7:9). The Jewish festival of Hanukkah remembers the rededication of the temple by the Maccabees in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52–59), and John mentions Jesus in the temple at "the feast of Dedication" (John 10:22).

a: from Lebo-hamath down to the Brook of Egypt
p: These are the ideal borders of the promised land.
b: Lebo-hamath ("the entrance of Hamath") was in the Beqaa valley of Lebanon, at the northern border promised in Numbers 34:8. The Brook of Egypt is the Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai: "the border will turn to the Wadi of Egypt and end at the sea" (Numbers 34:5). The whole promised land is gathered at Jerusalem.

a: On the eighth day he let the people go
t: Fourteen days and the eighth day
p: Chronicles explains: seven days to dedicate the altar, seven for the feast, and a closing gathering.
b: Leviticus adds an eighth day to the seven days of Booths, "the closing assembly" (Leviticus 23:36). Chronicles explains Solomon's festival as seven days to dedicate the altar, then seven days of the feast, then the people sent home on the twenty-third day of the month (2 Chronicles 7:8–10). Kings is briefer, and the "eighth day" here probably means the day after the second week. On the Greek, which lacks "and then seven days more, fourteen days," see the variant on 8:65.
